analysis.one_liner: Required every state to guarantee health insurance coverage to all its residents by 1994.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in two House committees from November 1991 until the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state to adopt and operate a plan guaranteeing health insurance to all residents by January 1, 1994. States could choose a fully public single-payer system or an employer-based system in which companies with 50 or more workers had to enroll employees and families in coverage or pay so they could enroll. Every plan had to cover a broad package of services, ban preexisting-condition exclusions, and charge low-income people little or nothing; states that refused to act would risk losing federal Medicaid money.
analysis.who_benefits: People without health insurance, especially those locked out because of preexisting conditions, low-income households (the state would pay their premiums and out-of-pocket costs below the poverty line), small-business owners and the self-employed (insurance pools plus a rising self-employed tax deduction reaching 100% by 1996), and health care providers who would gain millions of insured patients.

how_it_helps.text: Required each state to have a plan in place and operating by January 1, 1994 ensuring health insurance coverage for all residents, with federal planning and operating grants to help [S2][S3].
Banned health plans from excluding or limiting anyone because of a preexisting condition [S2][S3].
Required states to pay the full premiums, deductibles, copays, and coinsurance of anyone below the poverty line, and to limit those costs for everyone else [S3].

Mandated a broad benefit package: hospital and physician care, prescription drugs, long-term care including nursing home and home health, mental health care (at least 45 inpatient days and 20 outpatient visits a year), prenatal and well-baby care, and immunizations, with no dollar or duration limits on core services [S3].

Required employers with 50 or more workers to enroll employees and their families in a qualifying plan or contribute so they could enroll, and created insurance pools to make coverage affordable for the self-employed, the unemployed, and workers at small firms [S2][S3].
Raised the federal tax deduction for self-employed health insurance costs from 25% to 50% by 1994-95 and 100% by 1996, and made it permanent [S2][S3].
Offered extra federal payments to at least two states that adopted a single-payer system covering everyone, and made Medicare honor alternate state hospital payment systems [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large employers would bear new premium obligations for workers and their families; taxpayers would fund federal grants to states, higher Medicaid payments, and the single-payer bonuses; and health insurers would lose practices like preexisting-condition exclusions while gaining tens of millions of required customers.

drawbacks.text: The employer mandate would impose significant new costs on companies with 50 or more workers, a cost some could pass to workers through lower wages or slower hiring [S3].

The bill barred states from restricting managed care practices — plans could freely select providers, limit their networks, and steer patients to participating providers — preempting state consumer-protection rules and entrenching the managed care model [S3].

Tying federal Medicaid payments to adoption of a state universal-coverage plan would put pressure on states to accept a federal template, and the plan's scope (covering long-term care, mental health, and drugs for everyone) raised substantial cost questions the bill left to states to solve [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise — universal coverage with a generous benefit package, no preexisting-condition exclusions, and near-free care for the poor — was large and direct for ordinary people, paid for mainly by employers and taxpayers. The bill's weakest feature was its embrace of managed care: it handcuffed states from limiting network restrictions and utilization controls, the very mechanisms that later drove public frustration with HMOs. It was also a demanding mandate on states with a tight 1994 deadline and flexible, partly unfunded cost-control duties.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 1991 and sent to two House committees, then to subcommittees, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. David Obey introduced the bill on November 25, 1991, and it was referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees [S1][S5].
On January 14, 1992 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness and the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment — the last recorded action [S5].
No markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action is recorded before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care companies kept operating without a universal-coverage mandate or a ban on preexisting-condition exclusions, and large employers avoided new coverage obligations. Millions of uninsured Americans gained nothing; the country entered the 1992 election year and the 103rd Congress still without universal coverage.

for.name: David Obey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Universal Health Insurance Act of 1991 requiring states to guarantee coverage for all residents by 1994.

for.name: Reps. Swift and Kolter
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only two cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral on November 25, 1991; no markup or hearing on the bill is recorded and it was sent to a subcommittee, where it died.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, which handles tax and Medicare-Medicaid legislation, received the joint referral and took no recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only record of support is three Democratic sponsors, with no Republican cosponsorship and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have made private health benefit plans the permanent channel for universal coverage, mandating tens of millions of new customers, while banning preexisting-condition exclusions and limiting cost-sharing. Insurers would gain a locked-in market but lose underwriting practices that let them avoid sick customers.

The bill barred states from restricting managed care plans' ability to select providers, limit networks, and steer enrollees, preempting state consumer protections. HMOs were also exempted from a requirement that carriers offer a managed care plan to small employers.
Employers of 50 or more people would have had to enroll employees and families in qualifying coverage or contribute to it. The industry's cost would have been the coverage ordinary workers gained.
Universal coverage would have reduced uncompensated care and brought paying patients, including for long-term care and prescription drugs. Providers would benefit alongside the newly insured.
